claims.text: W38Ta36Cr15V11 films can be produced by magnetron sputtering with a bimodal nanocrystalline and ultrafine grain-size distribution.
The unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy has a single-phase BCC structure before irradiation.
Cr and V segregate to grain boundaries and triple junctions in the unmodified alloy.
Adding approximately 2 atomic % Zr during deposition will cause Zr to segregate preferentially to grain boundaries and irradiation-induced defect sinks.
The Zr addition will form Zr-enriched grain-boundary complexions.
Zr-enriched grain boundaries will reduce Cr and V mobility and impede their segregation and clustering.
Reduced Cr and V mobility will inhibit nucleation and growth of Cr/V-rich precipitates during irradiation.
Cr/V-rich second-phase regions in unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 evolve from lamella-like regions toward quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation.
The unmodified alloy shows no irradiation-created dislocation loops up to approximately 8 dpa.
The unmodified alloy has an as-deposited hardness of about 14 GPa and near-negligible irradiation hardening.
Approximately equal point-defect mobilities are the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance of unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Zr segregation will preserve the balanced point-defect recombination needed for negligible irradiation hardening.
At approximately 8 dpa, the Zr-modified alloy will have at least 50% less Cr/V-rich precipitate volume fraction or number density than the unmodified alloy.
The irradiation-induced defect density in the Zr-modified alloy will be similar to or slightly below that in the unmodified alloy.
The Zr-modified alloy will retain a sub-1 GPa irradiation-induced hardness increment.
Zr-enriched grain boundaries will stabilize the nanocrystalline grain network.
The Zr addition will improve thermal stability during bulk processing and thereby improve suitability for sintering or additive manufacturing.
Irradiation with 4–5 MeV ions at 500–600°C up to approximately 8 dpa represents the applicable fusion-service boundary for the intervention.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the intervention will prevent radiation-induced precipitate formation, whereas the quantitative prediction only requires at least a 50% reduction and therefore allows substantial residual precipitation.
